title: The Listening Cellar
premise: Vesper Thornbury, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise Hollowmere House, a derelict estate whose measurements refuse to stay constant and whose cellar hums with a song no one has written down. Waiting on the porch is Wren, the imaginary friend Vesper invented at age seven — unchanged, patient, and no longer imaginary. The house was built by a congregation that sang a four-verse hymn to bind something beneath the cellar; three verses survive in the walls, and the fourth exists only in the memory of those who were taken. As Vesper documents the house's impossible geometry, he discovers his own childhood was the missing verse: the congregation used children as vessels for songs too dangerous for adult voices. To escape, Vesper must learn the last verse without ever singing it aloud, while Wren — who is either his protector or the house's oldest lure — grows more desperate to make him open his mouth. In the end, Vesper writes the final verse into his survey report instead of singing it, sealing it in ink rather than breath; the house accepts the document as its prayer, releases him, and takes Wren down into the cellar in his place.
about_author: Sebastian Sandoval is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned properties across the American Northeast before turning to fiction. He claims every haunted house in his books is drawn from a real appraisal, though he has never said which ones.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Vesper. A bank hires him to appraise Hollowmere House, abandoned since 1974, with strict instructions to document everything and enter nothing twice. Vesper, whose rituals of measurement keep his loneliness at bay, arrives with instruments and notebooks. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking dread as the house appears larger from inside than out.

chapters.title: Figures That Don't Hold
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. His laser measurements of the ground floor disagree with each other by inches that grow each time he rechecks. He finds pencil marks on a doorframe recording a child's height — dated next Tuesday. Emotional beat: professional denial cracking into fascination; documentation begins to feel less like control and more like conversation.

chapters.title: The Man on the Porch
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Leaving at dusk, he finds a small figure waiting on the porch steps: Wren, the imaginary friend he invented at seven, wearing the same corduroy coat, unaged. Wren says only, 'You came back slower than I hoped.' Emotional beat: vertigo of recognition; the past arriving punctual as an appointment.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Friends Remember
chapters.summary: Alternating present and childhood flashback. Wren explains he waited where Vesper left him, and that the house 'kept the light on.' Vesper demands explanations; Wren offers only warnings about the cellar and its song. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into suspicion — is Wren protecting him or herding him?

chapters.title: The Congregation of the Open Throat
chapters.summary: Research chapter, Vesper's POV at the county archive. He learns Hollowmere was built by a splinter sect that believed certain entities could only be bound by hymns sung by children, whose voices 'haven't learned to lie.' Three members vanished in 1974; the fourth, a girl named Ada Lune, was never found. Emotional beat: scholarly thrill giving way to personal horror.

chapters.title: Down the First Stair
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Against Wren's pleading, he enters the cellar: a round chamber with four niches carved into the walls, each holding a music stand. The air hums a melody he almost recognizes. His recorder captures forty minutes of singing; playback lasts four seconds. Emotional beat: awe weaponized into compulsion.

chapters.title: Verse One, Written in Plaster
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Behind peeling plaster he finds Verse One of the binding hymn scored in handwriting that matches his own. When he copies it into his notebook, the house's measurements stabilize for one hour. Emotional beat: intoxicating discovery — the terrible sense that the house wants to be documented.

chapters.title: The Bank Calls It Condemned
chapters.summary: External pressure chapter. Vesper's supervisor orders him to file a preliminary report; the bank wants demolition approval. Veper stalls, lying for the first time in his career, claiming structural ambiguities need further study. Emotional beat: loyalty to truth bending under loyalty to the house — power beginning to corrupt through small permissions.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren's perspective surfaces for the first time. He confesses he was not invented but assigned: the congregation gave each child a 'listener' who would remember the verses if the child forgot. Wren remembers all four. If Vesper sings them, they both go free. Emotional beat: desperate love braided with manipulation; the reader can no longer tell which.

chapters.title: Ada Lune, Age Nine
chapters.summary: Vesper finds Ada Lune alive — sort of — living in the town's care home, ninety years old and still nine in her speech. She sings him fragments of Verse Two and warns: 'The house doesn't want your voice, boy. It wants your agreement.' Emotional beat: grief and pity; the cost of surviving a song.

chapters.title: Verse Two, Sung by Someone Else
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He transcribes Verse Two from Ada's broken recitation. That night the house plays it back through the pipes in a child's voice, note-perfect, and every door in the house stands open by exactly one inch. Emotional beat: violation — the house demonstrating it can use voices, including his.

chapters.title: The Measurements Turn Hostile
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The house begins editing his documents: his notes rewrite themselves, his photographs show rooms he never entered, and one photo shows himself asleep in the cellar chair. The bank threatens to send another surveyor. Emotional beat: paranoia tightening; documentation now a battlefield.

chapters.title: A Second Surveyor
chapters.summary: New POV: Marcus Webb, the replacement appraiser, arrives confident and dismissive. Vesper tries to warn him off; Marcus laughs, enters the cellar, and comes up humming a tune he can't name. Emotional beat: dread by proxy — watching someone walk willingly into the trap you nearly escaped.

chapters.title: Humming Is Not Singing
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Marcus deteriorates over two days, humming constantly, sleeping in the cellar. Wren tells Vesper the song needs four voices and Marcus is being tuned. Vesper must choose: save Marcus and lose his access, or let the house prepare its choir. Emotional beat: moral corrosion — Vesper chooses the house, and hates himself cleanly.

chapters.title: Verse Three, Found in a Child's Mouth
chapters.summary: Marcus, hollow-eyed, sings Verse Three unprompted in the kitchen. Vesper transcribes it while Marcus's voice splits into harmony with itself. Afterward Marcus remembers nothing and asks when he can go home. Emotional beat: horror at intimacy — the song using a stranger's body to teach itself to Vesper.

chapters.title: The Fourth Niche
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He realizes the fourth niche's music stand bears fresh scratches spelling his childhood nickname. The house has been waiting for him since 1974; Ada escaped because she refused to be the vessel, and the vacancy never filled. Wren begs him to leave tonight. Emotional beat: claustrophobic destiny — every exit now looks like a door in the house's wall.

chapters.title: What Vesper Forgot at Seven
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter. Seven-year-old Vesper, visiting Hollowmere with his mother — a congregation descendant — was offered as the fourth vessel but hid in the cellar and bit the hand that led him down. Wren was left behind to wait. Emotional beat: devastating recontextualization; his whole life of careful distance was flight from this house.

chapters.title: The Choir Assembles
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. The house seals its doors; Ada dies peacefully in her sleep mid-hum; Marcus descends the stairs singing; the bank's demolition permit is approved for Friday. Wren tells Vesper the truth at last: if Vesper sings the fourth verse, the thing below wakes free, and Wren becomes its mouth forever. Emotional beat: betrayal and clarity arriving together.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, the night before demolition. He coaxes the fourth verse out of the house itself — listening to the cellar hum, writing it down note by note without letting a single syllable pass his lips, biting a leather strap against the urge. Emotional beat: agonized discipline; the hardest work of his life done in silence.

chapters.title: The Demolition Morning
chapters.summary: Climax. The crew arrives; the house will not let the machines start. Vesper walks in past Marcus's empty clothes, descends to the cellar, and offers the house a trade: the complete hymn, all four verses, transcribed and signed — a document instead of a voice. The house considers. Wren, weeping, tells him to run. Emotional beat: white-knuckle stillness before the choice.

chapters.title: Ink Instead of Breath
chapters.summary: Climax resolved. The house accepts the document — paper is also a kind of prayer — and the cellar opens like a throat swallowing. Vesper shoves the notebook across the floor and runs as the walls take Wren gently down, the last verse sealed in ink, the entity bound to paper rather than freed by voice. The house collapses inward behind him. Emotional beat: triumph purchased with grief.

chapters.title: Filed and Closed
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Vesper's POV. He files the appraisal marked 'structure unsound, recommend preservation,' ensuring no one builds there again. At his desk he measures his office twice and gets the same number both times — then once, late at night, hears a faint humming he does not join. On his shelf, a corduroy button he kept. Emotional beat: bittersweet belonging — he finally belongs somewhere, and it costs him Wren.
